analysis.one_liner: Creates a USDA investigator with subpoena power to prosecute unfair meatpacking practices.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Agriculture Committee with bipartisan support in July 2022 and sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: A handful of meatpacking companies buy most of the nation's cattle, hogs, and poultry, and ranchers and growers have long argued they are paid unfairly low prices. This bill would create a dedicated Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters inside the Department of Agriculture, with the power to issue subpoenas and to sue meatpackers and live poultry dealers that violate the Packers and Stockyards Act, a 1921 fair-competition law. It passed the Senate Agriculture Committee with bipartisan support but never came up for a vote on the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and poultry growers, who could bring complaints against the large packers and dealers that buy their animals, and consumers, if stronger enforcement of buying and competition rules helps lower meat prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ranchers, poultry growers, and meat shoppers

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters within the Department of Agriculture, headed by a senior career employee, focused on competition and trade practices in the food and agriculture sector.
Gives the investigator power to use all available tools, including subpoenas, to investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act of 1921 by packers and live poultry dealers.

Grants the office authority to bring civil or administrative actions authorized under the Packers and Stockyards Act directly against packers and live poultry dealers, rather than leaving every case to the Justice Department.
Makes the office a liaison to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission on competition in the food and agricultural sector, coordinating enforcement across agencies.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies and live poultry dealers, who would face a dedicated investigator with subpoena power and direct lawsuits for unfair buying practices and anti-competitive conduct.

drawbacks.text: The investigator's lawsuit authority is limited to entities regulated under the Packers and Stockyards Act, so it cannot reach conduct by firms outside that law, and the office coordinates with, rather than replaces, the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, raising questions about whether a new office adds much to existing enforcement.

A new office with a staff of attorneys and investigators is a real cost to taxpayers, and critics of the approach argued that the Agriculture Department and Justice Department already hold subpoena and enforcement powers under the Packers and Stockyards Act; the bill's answer is concentration and dedicated attention, not new legal tools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does not create new rights or rewrite competition law; it creates a dedicated office with staff and subpoena power to actually enforce a 1921 law that ranchers say has been enforced weakly against a highly concentrated meatpacking industry. The taxpayer cost of a small office is modest next to the stakes: meat prices at the grocery store and the prices ranchers receive for cattle and poultry. Its main weakness is that it stays within the boundaries of existing law, so its impact depends entirely on how aggressively the office is run.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Agriculture Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate's legislative calendar in July 2022, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on March 17, 2022, with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Republican Senators Chuck Grassley, John Thune, and John Hoeven alongside Democrats like Cory Booker and Amy Klobuchar.
The Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee held a hearing on the bill on April 26, 2022.
On June 22, 2022, the committee ordered the bill to be reported favorably with an amendment, and on July 11, 2022, Chairwoman Stabenow reported it to the Senate with amendments.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 436) on July 11, 2022, meaning it was waiting for floor time.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies and live poultry dealers came out ahead, because a dedicated investigator with subpoena power to sue them under the Packers and Stockyards Act was never created. Ranchers, growers, and shoppers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large meatpackers and live poultry dealers

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split: 6 of 50 Senate Republicans and 6 of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsored, and the committee reported the bill favorably; the bill died without a floor vote, so no vote split ever happened.

industries.note: The bill gives a dedicated USDA investigator subpoena power and direct authority to sue packers for violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act, raising enforcement risk for the few firms that dominate cattle and hog buying. Ranchers and shoppers benefit if that enforcement leads to fairer prices.

The reported bill extends the investigator's lawsuit authority to live poultry dealers, the companies that contract with poultry growers. Growers, who say dealers control their pay and inputs, would gain a direct avenue to challenge unfair treatment.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and poultry growers
industries.note: Ranchers and growers would get a dedicated office with subpoena power to investigate and prosecute unfair practices by the packers and dealers who buy their animals. Their interest runs alongside consumers', since more competition in livestock buying can lower meat prices.
